chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdullah, from his father, from Khalaf ibn Hammad, from Muhraz, from Abu Baseer, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Debts are of three types: A man who has a debt owed to him, so he grants respite; and when he has a debt owed to him, he gives it and does not delay, so that is for him and not against him. And a man who, when he has a debt owed to him, demands full payment; and when he has a debt owed to him, he pays it in full, so that is neither for him nor against him. And a man who, when he has a debt owed to him, demands full payment; and when he has a debt owed to him, he delays payment, so that is against him and not for him.'
ai.seo_question: What are the three types of debtors and creditors in Shia Islamic teachings?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi categorizes debtors and creditors into three ethical archetypes, highlighting the superior virtue of the one who combines leniency in collecting debts with promptness in repaying them. In Shia jurisprudence, this reflects the principle of 'Ihsan' (excellence) in financial transactions, where being 'for oneself' implies gaining spiritual and social merit, while being 'against oneself' denotes loss of status. The text underscores the moral weight of delay ('tatil') in repayment, a key concept in Islamic commercial ethics.
